The skill you'll use most as a software engineer is the one almost nobody teaches: reading code you didn't write.  A 2018 study that tracked 78 professional developers over 3,148 working hours found they spent 58% of their time just understanding code.

Most of us learned by writing programs from a blank file. Most jobs start you in someone else's. 

 And that was before AI. In September, developers started more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub with an AI agent, according to GitHub's latest Octoverse report. 

Writing code got cheap. Someone still has to read all of it.  Start where the program starts.

↳ Find the entry point and follow one real request all the way through.. Run it before you read it.
↳ Ten minutes with a debugger and a breakpoint will teach you more than an hour of scrolling.. Read the tests.
↳ They're the closest thing to a spec most codebases have. Use git blame to find out why.
↳ The commit and the PR behind a weird line usually explain it better than any comment.. Write down what you learn as you go.
↳ A rough map of how things fit together helps you now, and the next new person even more.

 How do you get your head around a codebase you've never seen before?

If your developers are using AI tools to write code faster, your testing needs to keep pace, or defects will reach production faster too. 

The productivity gains from AI-assisted development are certainly real. However, faster coding also means more code to test, and some of that code will be written by developers who understand AI-generated logic less well than logic they wrote themselves. 
Strengthening your quality engineering around code production can protect any productivity gain, because clear acceptance criteria, automated checks in the delivery pipeline, and code reviews that question what the code is meant to do can then catch problems at the same pace the code is produced. 

That becomes even more important where AI-assisted development is being used at scale, of course, and that's why Assured Thought's quality engineers work closely with Izertis’s software engineering teams.  
They combine AI-assisted development with DevSecOps practices, while we bring the quality engineering discipline that helps regulated firms deliver faster without compromising quality. 

Faster delivery only benefits your firm if what you release can be trusted. We can help with that.

In a hedge fund or proprietary trading firm, a few microseconds can matter. The person building the system behind them matters just as much.

There's a reason technical hiring in this part of the market is so specialised.
You're not simply looking for a good software engineer. You're looking for someone who understands what happens when latency, execution speed, data quality and system reliability can all have a direct impact on trading performance.

A C++ engineer working on a low-latency trading platform, a quant developer building execution systems or an infrastructure specialist keeping critical systems running all bring something very specific to the table.

And finding that combination of technical depth and relevant experience isn't always straightforward.

The distinction matters when hiring. Someone can have an impressive engineering background and still have very little exposure to the demands of a trading environment.

For firms competing in hedge funds and proprietary trading, understanding the technology is only part of it. Understanding where that person has applied it, and the environment they've worked in, can make all the difference.

In this market, the right technical experience isn't just a nice addition to the CV. It's often the reason someone gets the conversation.

GitHub invited me to join a group of companies from the Nordics 🇩🇰🇸🇪🇳🇴🇫🇮, and it was an amazing experience from start to finish.
A BIG thank you to Amr Al Jarhi andÖmür Sert from GitHub for giving me this opportunity 🙏 Thanks to you, I got to connect with amazing people from the Nordics and from all over the world. The conversations we had between sessions were just as valuable as the sessions themselves 🤝💡

What stayed with me most was seeing how companies everywhere are trying to change their whole SDLC with agents 🤖
There’s a clear gap between companies right now:
🔹 Agents that write code were the first step, and many companies are still working through it.
🔹 Others have already taken the next step: agents working in development loops, grounded in company knowledge, with autonomous testing and quality assurance. Engineers get involved when they’re really needed, not for every single change ⚡

I lovedSimona Toader’s session on automating PR quality with Copilot CLI and GitHub Actions. It was a great real-world example of how AI and automation can keep quality high at scale without a human checking every change 👏
In the opening keynote, Jay Parikh showed something that stuck with me 📈 Merged PRs, commits and new repos on GitHub grew linearly for years. Then around mid-2025, when agents arrived, all three curves started growing exponentially. Today that’s 220M merged PRs, 7.38B commits and 30.3M new repos every month 🤯

Software engineering is not solved, but it has fundamentally changed 🔥
I’d love to have a conversation with anyone who has a take on where this is heading. What does the future of software engineering look like to you? 👇

New process, new software , a reorganisation as well as a new governance framework?

Each has a sponsor, a business case and a launch date. Each makes sense on its own and each lands on the same Engineers, in the same quarter, on top of the day job.

So is anyone looking at the holistic impact?

Usually not. Initiatives are owned by different functions, planned in isolation and judged on their own success criteria. Nobody owns the total load on the people at the end of the chain, and nobody is checking how the initiatives interact.

That matters, because change initiatives can work against each other. A new tool is built around a process that’s about to be replaced. A reorganisation cuts across a governance framework launching next month. Each can be sound, but the combination can still be damaging.

Engineers will recognise this as a systems problem. We would never assess components in isolation and declare the whole system sound. We look at interfaces, interactions and cumulative loading. Yet we routinely do the opposite with change.

What helps:

- Map everything landing on your teams in one place

- Quantify the real hours each initiative demands

- Check the interfaces between initiatives for dependencies and contradictions

- Sequence, don’t stack

- Stop something. If nothing has been dropped, the capacity doesn’t exist

A change portfolio nobody manages as a whole is just a set of good ideas competing for the same people, and occasionally colliding.

How many change initiatives are landing on your team right now, and who is looking at how they fit together?

posts.text:
Code is cheap now. Keeping up with the cutting edge is not.

I often see engineering groups build complete in-house solutions, AI-enabled or for AI, to problems the whole industry is working on. It's usually the result of a few things:

1. Creating a POC is easy, which makes it look like building and maintaining the full system is easy too.
2. These are the most exciting problems in the field: software factories and the SDLC, context engines, evaluation frameworks. It's natural that good engineers want to work on them.
3. Building needs no approval. Adopting an outside tool means security, legal and budget.
4. Nothing existed when they started. A few months later, something did.

And it's true: an internally developed solution is easier to justify than ever, because it's easier than ever to create and maintain one. That also makes it more OK than ever to build one.

But even if maintaining it seems easy, maintaining it at the pace of innovation is not. In AI engineering the cutting edge moves at insane speed, and the best solution today may be completely different tomorrow.

Now that "code is cheap", it's easy to forget that software engineering, and the AI engineering built on it, is at its core the design of robust, maintainable, innovative systems. That design is what you'd have to keep redoing, and it's as hard as it ever was.

So before you build from scratch:

→ Understand if the need is real.
→ Understand why the industry hasn't solved it yet. It's probably hard.
→ Understand how you'll measure success. When a hard problem looks solved quickly, the measurement is usually what's wrong.
→ Be ready to throw it away. You probably won't be able to compete with what the industry and open source ship next.

My point is simple: don't build a complete in-house solution unless you actually need one. Most of the time you can take an existing solution, open source or bought, and build what you need on top of it.

And if the need isn't urgent and no outside solution exists yet, you can be sure someone is working on it. Maybe the right thing to do is wait. Waiting isn't losing. It's winning somewhere else. Not forever, just until you can't wait.

There is always somewhere else. I can promise you that your organization has more than enough problems of its own, whether that's enabling AI or solving something with it.

That's where your most valuable resource belongs: the engineers who are capable of designing such systems. Put them on your own problems, and build on what already exists everywhere else. That is the key to keeping up with innovation, as it always was.

Last week I asked how you trust an agent-built system. Here is the step before that.

Many people I talk to think agentic software is traditional software with model calls in it.

I see three groups in small and mid-sized companies right now.

The first uses nothing yet. Some by choice, most because they do not know where to start, or how to get around all the internal and external rules.

The second lets a model write most of the code. You architect the model calls, steer it, ask for changes and ask for tests. You still decide every step and you own the system. This is a sensible way in, and it is where most of the work I see happens.

The third lets the agent decide the steps. It writes and changes the system inside a harness, which picks the model for each task, makes the plan and keeps notes between runs. What runs can be ordinary software; the agent is its engineer. In the second group you steer the model. In the third, the agent steers itself.

That changes what you have to check. In the second, you see every change and ask for the tests. In the third, the agent's own code, plan and even its choice of model change with every change it makes. Its own tests passing is not enough. You need a check from outside that sees every change and looks again at work that already passed.

There is a second question for a small company: where does the model run? Some start local, on their own hardware, because the data stays in the house. Some start with a frontier model, because it can do more today. Many will end up with both: the strong model builds, and once the system is tested, a cheaper one may be able to run it. The harness decides, and that choice needs checking too.

None of the three is wrong as a starting point. The mistake is not knowing which one you are in.

Which of the three is your company in?

If AI cuts the effort it takes to build software, what should a client expect from an engineering team?

At The AI Meetup Sri Lanka, Edition 2, hosted by Gapstars, our founder Premuditha Perera spoke about how AI is changing the economics of producing software. He gave a familiar example from client proposals: this requires X engineers for Y months.

"I think engineers need to move up the problem stack." He pointed to where that starts: before the code. What problem are we actually solving? Which architecture decisions will be hard to reverse? Once the software is running, how will we know it solved the problem? These used to be questions for architects and CTOs. Increasingly, they're every engineer's job.

As Premuditha put it, "As AI helps solve the problems we’ve traditionally been solving, we need to change the problems we solve."

Multilingual link building has a blind spot, and it is not the articles.

Teams translate the content carefully, then leave the account text in English. The profile on a Turkish site says the author is a software engineer from Austin. The comment on a Thai blog is in English. Everything around the link is localised except the thing posting it.

Two failure modes cause this:

1. The default profile and comment fields are never edited, so they stay English by definition.

Every client call goes well…

until I say, “We’re based in Pakistan.”

Then the questions change.

I lead staff augmentation at Veroke pvt. ltd.
a software company in Pakistan.
 
Most CTOs and engineering leaders in Europe are skeptical 
before I say much more. 
I think they’re right to be.

Many have hired offshore developers before and burned.
A team that said "YES" to everything.
Updates that sounded fine until the demo.
A remote engineer who went quiet after month two.

I don’t argue with that. 
It happens.

What I’ve learned is that skepticism isn’t the problem. 
Vague reassurance is.

“Our software engineers are top quality” means nothing. 
Every vendor says it.

What earns a skeptical engineering leader’s trust is specifics:
Who has this engineer shipped software for?
What did they do when the spec was wrong?
Who is accountable if it doesn’t work?

That last one matters most to me. 
Our company has been building software for clients for over 16 years.

The engineers we place come from real delivery teams, not a candidate database. 

When something breaks, there’s a team behind them that has seen it break before.

That isn’t a promise. 
It’s just a different starting point.

So if you’re skeptical of offshore engineering teams, keep it. 
Just aim it at a better question.

Not “where are they from?”
But “what have they been accountable for?”

Who develops tomorrow's senior engineers?

AI is changing how software gets built. But there's a question I think engineering leaders need to take more seriously:

If AI takes over much of the work traditionally done by junior engineers, how do we develop the next generation of senior engineers?

Senior engineers don't become senior simply by writing more code.

They develop judgment through experience.

They learn by debugging difficult problems, understanding trade-offs, making mistakes, reviewing decisions, and seeing the long-term consequences of their work.

AI can accelerate many of these activities. But acceleration doesn't automatically mean learning.

We may end up with smaller, highly productive teams of experienced engineers while gradually weakening the pipeline that creates them.

I don't think the answer is to preserve repetitive junior work just for the sake of training.

We need to redesign how engineers learn.

That means giving less experienced people meaningful problems, stronger mentorship, exposure to architectural decisions, and opportunities to validate AI-generated solutions.

The next generation of engineering organizations shouldn't optimize only for today's productivity.

They also need to build tomorrow's capabilities.

If you want to understand why Warp divergence serialization in custom CUDA compute kernels matters, you have to look past high-level code and inspect the compiled machine instructions and kernel tracepoints.

Profiling our 8x NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB cluster linked via 600GB/s NVLink 3.0 interconnect under a sustained 100k req/s load revealed why conditional if/else branches evaluated based on thread ID modulo 2 breaks down so violently at scale.

The Root Cause at the Silicon Level:
GPUs execute threads in lockstep warps of 32 threads using SIMT architecture. If threads in a warp take divergent code branches, both paths are executed serially while masking inactive threads.

The Telemetry Comparison (100k Concurrent Load):
- Baseline (conditional if/else branches evaluated based on thread ID modulo 2): 50% hardware execution efficiency as threads idle while opposite branch runs
- Tuned (data reorganization ensuring all 32 threads in a warp execute the same branch path): 100% active warp execution efficiency and 2.1x speedup in custom activation layer

The Production Action Plan:
Sort data arrays by branch condition prior to kernel launch or replace branch conditions with predication instructions (PTX selp) and min/max intrinsics.

Key Takeaway: High throughput is rarely just an algorithmic challenge in modern low-latency systems. It is almost always a cache coherence, memory bus arbitration, or kernel synchronization bottleneck.

I recently had the opportunity to attend the 2026 Academic Annual Conference of the Shanxi Provincial Society of Mechanical Engineering in Taiyuan, China.

The theme, “𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆–𝗘𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗠𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴,” highlighted university–industry partnerships, practical education and intelligent manufacturing.

One discussion focused on Outcome-Based Assessment (OBA) and professional accreditation. I learned that engineering education should be measured not only by what is taught, but by what graduates can demonstrate. This requires clear learning outcomes, reliable evidence, evaluation and continuous improvement.

Another key topic was industry–education integration. Universities cannot prepare engineers for modern industry in isolation. Collaboration through industrial projects, practical training and research is essential to connecting academic learning with workplace needs.

I was especially interested in the sessions on intelligent manufacturing and robotics. Presentations covered robotic precision, data collection, hand-pose detection, data processing and calibration. They showed how mechanical engineering is increasingly connected with artificial intelligence, computer vision, sensors and intelligent control.

Beyond the presentations, we visited facilities including the Intelligent Manufacturing Key Technology Engineering Research Centre, the Mechanical Engineering Experimental Centre and the Engineering Training Centre.

Seeing manufacturing equipment and robotic applications made the discussions more meaningful, connecting theory with practical applications.

As a Mechatronics and Automotive Engineer, I saw clear links between these developments and my interests in electric vehicles and intelligent transportation. Robotics and AI have important applications in automated vehicle manufacturing, autonomous systems, intelligent vehicle control, battery monitoring and delivery robots.

My main takeaway is that the future of engineering will require more than expertise in one discipline. It will depend on bringing mechanical systems, electronics, software and artificial intelligence together to develop practical solutions to real-world challenges.

I am grateful for the opportunity to learn from researchers and industry professionals.

This experience strengthened my interest in robotics, intelligent systems, electric vehicles and smart manufacturing. It reminded me that growth requires continuous learning and turning knowledge into practical solutions.

The journey of becoming a better engineer never stops.

Xero has started sending engineers into accounting firms. 

That tells you more about AI than any product launch this year.

Last week it launched a service that puts consultants and engineers alongside firms to design and build AI workflows inside the practice, starting with the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

Its own reasoning was refreshingly honest.

Many firms aren’t sure which tools to trust with client data, and they don’t have the capacity to build AI workflows themselves, so they stall.

That matches what I see when I talk to practices.

The tools have been good enough for a while now, and the bottleneck was never the software.

The harder part is that an engineer can only automate what the firm can actually explain.
If you ask most practices how they handle a new client’s year-end, you’ll get a different answer from every person in the office.

Nobody can build a workflow on top of that, however good the engineer is.

So the firms that get the most out of AI won’t be the ones with the biggest budgets or the newest tools.

They’ll be the ones that sat down and wrote out how they actually work before anyone arrived to automate it.

That job can’t be handed to Xero, or to anyone else.

If an engineer turned up at your firm tomorrow, could you show them how a piece of work gets done from start to finish?

I love graphs and enjoy preparing clear, publication-ready scientific plots. Therefore, I have created APlot (Data Visualizer)—an open-source, cross-platform desktop application built in Python (on top of Matplotlib, NumPy, and Pandas) designed to make creating 2D and 3D scientific graphs intuitive and fast.

Built through agentic AI andAI-assisted development, APlot progressed through ~85 commits over ten weeks to reach a stable, tested release (v1.6.0) ready for daily scientific workflows. I invite fellow researchers, engineers, and students to test the software and share feedback.   

Key advantages of APlot compared to other plotting software:
Full Excel-style spreadsheet built in: Unlike tools that treat data tables as static buffers, APlot supports multi-sheet workbooks, cell-level formulas (=A1+sin(B1/pi), $A$1+(1+0.1*randn())), drag-to-fill series generation, and one-click column math.

Instant secondary-axis toggles: Assign any column to the bottom/top X axis (x_B/x_T) or left/right Y axis (y_L/y_R) via checkboxes directly above the table—secondary axes appear and scale automatically without navigating nested menus.

True click-to-edit canvas: Every title, axis label, legend box, shape, arrow, and colorbar can be dragged, resized, rotated, or edited inline directly on the fixed-size page.

Publication defaults out of the box: Automatic axis bounds snap cleanly to major ticks across linear, log_10, log_2, and ln scales, paired with 13 2D and one 3D plot styles (including contour/pcolor fields and asymmetric error bars) and 8 built-in curve-fitting models with automatic starting guesses.

100% reproducible, stand-alone Python export: Beyond saving everything in a self-contained .aplt archive (with embedded PNG/PDF previews), APlot can export any figure as a stand-alone Python script requiring only numpy and matplotlib—no host application needed to re-run or customize the plot later.

Free, open-source, and single-file simple: Licensed under GNU GPL v3, running natively on macOS, Windows, and Linux via pre-built installers or a singleaplot.py file (Anaconda python is recommended under Mac).   

If you work with experimental or simulation data (CSV, TXT, DAT, Excel), feel free to download APlot, test it on your datasets, and share your thoughts on what works well or what features to add next.

In Indonesia, shopping spikes follow content, not just calendars. The Ministry of Trade reported that during Harbolnas 2025, 54% of consumers shopped through creator affiliate links and 80% used livestream features.

On Tokopedia and TikTok Shop’s 10.10 promo this year, transactions rose 9x and 4x respectively, according to the platforms.

For anyone running an online store, that changes how you plan for peak days:

• A spike can start in seconds, when a creator goes live or a flash sale opens, not on a schedule

• It doesn’t peak once. It peaks in waves, all day

• The checkout page takes the hit, not the product page

Three things that help:

1. Scale on demand, not on a timetable: auto-scaling that reacts in minutes, and is tested before the day
2. Protect checkout: queues and rate limits, so a wave slows people down instead of breaking things
3. Cache what you can: product pages, images and search results, ahead of the spike

If a creator sold out 10,000 units in ten minutes, what would happen to your checkout?

Norway and Indonesia Join Forces: Up to 12 Million Tonnes of Carbon Credits to Support Solar and Energy Storage Development

A new international climate partnership could unlock fresh financing opportunities for Indonesia's renewable energy sector.

On November 11, 2026, Indonesia and Norway signed a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) during COP31, advancing bilateral cooperation under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement.

Under the agreement, Norway will purchase up to 12 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emission reductionsgenerated by eligible solar energy projects developed by Indonesia's state-owned electricity company, PT PLN. The cooperation is expected to continue through 2038.

According to media reports, the indicative carbon credit price is estimated at USD 20–40 per tonne.

Solar + Storage Takes Centre Stage
Beyond international carbon credit trading, the agreement aims to establish an additional financing mechanism for renewable energy development in Indonesia.

Key areas of focus include:
Floating Solar Projects: Supporting the development of solar PV installations, particularly floating solar facilities.
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS): Prioritising eligible renewable energy projects integrated with battery storage.
Generation-Based Incentives: Providing additional financial incentives linked to electricity generation, helping improve project economics and investment attractiveness.

By combining solar generation with battery storage, projects can shift daytime renewable electricity to periods of higher demand, reduce reliance on fossil-fuel generation and improve grid flexibility.

Market Insight

Indonesia has significant solar energy potential, but project development continues to face challenges related to financing, grid integration and investment returns.

This partnership highlights an emerging financing model: turning verified emission reductions into an additional revenue stream for renewable energy projects.

By connecting international carbon markets with solar and energy storage investments, the agreement could help improve project bankability and encourage greater private-sector participation.

For renewable energy developers, EPC contractors and battery storage suppliers, Indonesia's evolving carbon financing framework presents an opportunity worth monitoring.

As Southeast Asia accelerates its energy transition, the integration of carbon markets, solar PV and BESS could become an increasingly important driver of renewable energy investment.
